strengths: UNOT addresses a useful problem: amortizing repeated fixed-cost optimal transport computations across datasets and grid resolutions. Combining neural operators, synthetic adversarial training, and inexpensive Sinkhorn targets is a well-motivated contribution.

The reported initializer results are strong. Table 4 shows approximately 1.3–2.8% transport-cost error after one Sinkhorn iteration, substantially outperforming Meta OT outside its training dataset while nearly matching it on MNIST. Table 2 reports 1.25–7.4× speedups over default initialization.

Evaluation spans several datasets, cross-dataset pairs, Euclidean and spherical costs, and multiple resolutions. The appendix includes marginal-violation convergence and quantitative barycenter comparisons, providing useful evidence beyond scalar cost prediction.

Proposition 5 provides a useful residual-to-potential error bound for fixed positive kernels. Detailed hyperparameters, training pseudocode, and links to code and model weights also support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central universality guarantee does not apply to the evaluated generator. Theorem 3 requires equal input/output dimensions and Lip(NN) < λ, whereas Appendix C uses a 200-dimensional latent variable to generate two 4096-entry measures and explicitly does not enforce the Lipschitz constraint. Its positive-density conclusion therefore cannot justify the implemented generator’s coverage. The manifold hypothesis does not repair this gap. Empirical transfer across image datasets is valuable, but does not establish the claimed ability to generate arbitrary discrete distributions.

The theoretical connection to the learned potentials needs reconciliation. Beyond the likely sign typo in Eq. (1), which subtracts rather than adds KL, Eq. (3) uses the reference measure μ⊗ν. Its discrete coupling consequently includes marginal-mass factors, whereas Proposition 1 and Algorithm 1 use entropy-based matrix-scaling potentials. These potentials differ by ε log marginal masses, so Proposition 2 does not directly establish convergence of the quantity actually predicted, g = ε log v. Algorithm 1 additionally labels ⟨C,Π⟩ as OTε despite omitting regularization. These are consequential distinctions for interpreting the theory and reported errors.

The downstream geometric algorithms contain substantive problems as written. Algorithm 3 applies softmax directly to updated probability masses; this is not projected gradient descent and moves a nonuniform optimum even when its gradient vanishes. Equation (11) omits the derivative of the outer Sinkhorn divergence’s self-interaction term, −½OTε(μ̂,μ̂). The actual implementations and objectives need clarification before the barycenter and gradient-flow conclusions can be assessed reliably. GeONet superiority is also supported only by a qualitative example.

The experiments do not isolate the contributions of adversarial generation and bootstrapping. Particularly informative controls would use a fixed synthetic generator and train the same predictor with the dual objective on matched data and compute. Comparing against Meta OT trained only on MNIST demonstrates transfer performance, but cannot establish whether the advantage comes from the proposed training mechanism or broader training-distribution coverage.

The strongest acceleration claim is supported only against default initialization, using a stopping threshold based on the unavailable ground-truth transport cost. Although marginal-violation curves are supplied, matched wall-clock comparisons against Gaussian and learned initializers at practical feasibility or optimality tolerances are missing. Tighter-accuracy measurements and an amortization analysis of the approximately 35-hour training cost would better establish practical significance.

strengths: UNOT offers a meaningful combination of neural operators, adversarially generated training measures, and bootstrapped Sinkhorn targets. Learning across datasets and resolutions is a useful extension of amortized optimal transport beyond dataset-specific predictors.

The empirical distance results are strong within the tested settings. Table 4 reports mean relative errors of 1.3–2.8% after one Sinkhorn iteration across six dataset pairings, substantially outperforming Meta OT outside its MNIST training distribution while nearly matching its MNIST performance.

The evaluation extends beyond scalar distance prediction: marginal-constraint violations improve, Table 6 reports better barycenter accuracy than both baseline initializations, and Table 2 includes inference overhead when reporting speedups up to 7.4×.

Predicting one dual potential and using inexpensive Sinkhorn refinement is well motivated. The appendix supplies substantial implementation details, resolution and regularization experiments, and links to code and model weights.
weaknesses: The claimed universality is not established for the implemented generator. Theorem 3 requires equal input/output dimensions and a Lipschitz bound below the skip coefficient. Appendix C instead uses 200 latent dimensions to generate 8192 output values and explicitly does not enforce the Lipschitz condition. Acknowledging these differences does not justify the subsequent assertion that the generator cannot bottleneck generalization. Moreover, positive density for an idealized generator would not establish uniform prediction accuracy.

The mathematical formulation mixes distinct OT objectives and potential conventions. Equation (1) incorrectly subtracts KL divergence, while Algorithm 1 reports only the transport-cost component as OTϵ. After correcting the sign, the KL dual in Equation (3) implies Πij = μiνj exp((fi + gj − Cij)/ϵ), whereas Proposition 1 and the learned scaling potentials omit the marginal factors. Consequently, Proposition 2's convergence result does not directly justify the variables actually predicted without an explicit transformation. The sign is readily correctable, but the potential mismatch and evaluated objective require substantive clarification.

The downstream geometry calculations contain consequential errors. Equation (11) omits the derivative of the outer self-interaction term −½OTϵ(μ̂, μ̂), so it does not differentiate the stated nested Sinkhorn divergence; Appendix A.4 repeats this omission. Algorithm 3 also applies softmax directly to probability weights after a gradient step, which is not a simplex projection and generally changes a nonuniform measure even when its gradient is zero. These issues undermine the interpretation and reproducibility of the corresponding demonstrations.

The experiments do not isolate the benefits of the proposed training ingredients. There is no controlled comparison against a fixed or random generator, or against the Meta OT dual-objective loss trained on the same synthetic distributions. The MNIST-trained Meta OT comparison demonstrates useful transfer, but confounds training-distribution coverage with architectural and loss improvements. The MLP variant is described without matched quantitative comparisons.

The broad efficiency claim exceeds the timing evidence. Table 2 compares against the default initialization using an oracle stopping threshold based on ground-truth cost error. Although the appendix includes marginal-violation curves, it does not report runtime at common practical feasibility tolerances or matched timings against competing initializations. The substantial training cost—approximately 35 H100 hours per cost-specific model—also needs an amortization analysis to establish when the approach delivers an overall computational advantage.

strengths: The combination of Fourier neural operators, adversarially generated measure pairs, and bootstrapped Sinkhorn targets is a meaningful contribution to amortized OT. It addresses the useful setting of repeated problems with a fixed cost and varying grid resolutions.

The reported generalization results are strong within the tested setting. Table 4 shows mean transport-cost errors of 1.3–2.8% across six dataset combinations, substantially outperforming MNIST-trained Meta OT outside MNIST while remaining competitive on MNIST.

The evaluation includes three cost/domain settings, resolution sweeps, marginal constraint violations, and quantitative barycenter comparisons. Timings include neural inference and demonstrate speedups up to 7.4× over default initialization.

Proposition 5 provides a useful fixed-problem justification for bootstrapped targets through a contraction-based residual bound. The appendices provide substantial training detail and links to code and model weights.
weaknesses: The central universality claim is not established for the implemented generator. Theorem 3 requires equal input/output dimensions and Lip(NN) < lambda, whereas Appendix C uses 200 latent coordinates to generate up to 8192 weights and explicitly does not enforce the Lipschitz condition. Acknowledging these differences does not justify the subsequent assertion that generator coverage cannot bottleneck performance. Moreover, full support of an idealized generator would not establish finite-sample accuracy across all measures.

The OT definitions and learned potentials need substantive reconciliation. Beyond the apparent KL sign typo in Equation (1), Algorithm 1 reports only the linear transport cost while the stated objective includes regularization. Also, epsilon times log(v) is an entropy-dual potential; the KL-relative-to-product-measures potentials in Equation (3) and Proposition 2 differ by marginal log terms. These distinctions affect the interpretation of reported errors and whether the convergence theorem applies to the actual training targets.

The downstream geometry claims contain mathematical and algorithmic problems. Equation (11), as stated for an outer Sinkhorn divergence, omits the derivative of the source self-interaction term. Algorithm 3 applies softmax directly to probability weights after a gradient step; this changes a nonuniform distribution even when its gradient vanishes and is not the claimed simplex projection. These formulas should be corrected and reconciled with the implementation. The claimed superiority over GeONet also needs aggregate geodesic errors beyond the single illustrated example.

The experiments do not isolate the contributions of adversarial generation, bootstrapping, and the FNO architecture. Comparing MNIST-trained Meta OT with UNOT trained on 200 million generated samples confounds architectural and objective improvements with training-distribution coverage and compute. Matched-data comparisons using the Meta OT loss and nonadversarial generators would substantially strengthen the explanation of why UNOT generalizes.

The efficiency evidence supports a narrower conclusion than the state-of-the-art claim. Table 2 measures time to a ground-truth cost-error threshold unavailable during deployment and compares only with default initialization; Gaussian timings are omitted in Appendix D.7. Timings at matched marginal-residual or optimality tolerances, comparisons using efficient grid kernels, and an amortization analysis of the approximately 35 H100-hours required per cost function are needed. The appendix's marginal-error plots are useful but do not establish these runtime conclusions.

strengths: UNOT addresses an important amortized computation problem. Combining Fourier neural operators, adversarially generated training distributions, and short Sinkhorn bootstrapping targets is a coherent contribution that extends fixed-resolution neural OT solvers.

The transport-cost results are strong across the tested datasets. Table 4 reports approximately 1.3–2.8% relative error after one Sinkhorn iteration, substantially outperforming Gaussian initialization and approaching MNIST-trained Meta OT on MNIST without training on that dataset.

The empirical support extends beyond scalar cost prediction: marginal-constraint violations improve, Table 6 shows better MNIST barycenters, and Table 2 reports actual runtime improvements of 1.25–7.4 times over default initialization. Resolution sweeps and spherical experiments further demonstrate useful flexibility.

The manuscript provides extensive implementation details, pseudocode, supplementary experiments, and a link to code and weights. Proposition 5 supplies a useful residual-to-potential-error bound under its assumptions.
weaknesses: The central universality guarantee does not cover the implemented generator. Theorem 3 requires equal input/output dimensions and a residual branch with Lipschitz constant below the skip coefficient. Appendix C instead uses a 200-dimensional latent input to generate 8192 output values and explicitly does not enforce the Lipschitz condition. The theorem therefore cannot establish the claimed full-dimensional density or universal coverage for this implementation. Even the idealized support result does not establish adequate coverage under finite training. Likewise, Proposition 5 establishes an error bound, not convergence of the stopped-gradient adversarial training procedure.

The mathematical formulations are not consistently connected. Equation (1) has a negative KL term, whereas the stated dual and Sinkhorn algorithm require positive KL regularization. More consequentially, for the KL-relative-to-product formulation in Equation (3), Proposition 1 requires u = μ ⊙ exp(f/ε) and v = ν ⊙ exp(g/ε). Omitting these marginal factors switches to entropy-based potentials. Consequently, Proposition 2's convergence result is not directly a justification for the learned ε log(v) target. Algorithm 1 also reports only ⟨C,Π⟩, rather than the regularized objective defined elsewhere. These distinctions must be resolved to clarify both the theoretical claims and the quantities evaluated.

The downstream geometry algorithms contain substantive errors as written. Algorithm 3 applies softmax directly to a probability vector after a gradient step; this is not the claimed projected gradient descent. Even at zero gradient, a nonuniform solution such as (0.9, 0.1) moves to approximately (0.69, 0.31). Equation (11) also omits the derivative of the outer Sinkhorn divergence's source self-interaction term. Corrected algorithms and verification that they reproduce the reported results are needed. The qualitative GeONet comparison on one interpolation provides limited additional assurance.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed components' contributions. There are no controlled comparisons against a fixed or random generator, or against the dual-objective loss using the same architecture and training distribution. Comparing UNOT's extensive synthetic training with MNIST-trained Meta OT demonstrates transfer performance, but does not establish whether the gains arise from the generator, bootstrapping objective, architecture, or training budget.

The state-of-the-art speed claim is stronger than the timing evidence. Runtime comparisons primarily use default initialization; Gaussian timing is omitted because the authors' implementation was slow, and matched Meta OT timings are absent. Timings target an oracle 1% ground-truth cost error rather than a practical stopping criterion. The appendix's marginal-feasibility curves are useful, but corresponding runtime comparisons and an amortization analysis of the approximately 35-hour training cost per model are missing.

strengths: UNOT presents a useful combination of neural operators, synthetic adversarial training, and bootstrapped Sinkhorn targets. Learning an initialization that transfers across datasets and resolutions is a meaningful extension of dataset-specific amortized OT, even though the underlying components build on established methods.

The empirical generalization results are encouraging. Across 500 evaluation pairs, Table 4 reports approximately 1.3–2.8% transport-cost error after one Sinkhorn iteration, substantially outperforming MNIST-trained Meta OT outside MNIST while nearly matching it on MNIST. Experiments cover multiple resolutions, three cost/domain settings, and a variable-regularization variant.

The evidence extends beyond scalar cost prediction: the appendix reports improved marginal feasibility and quantitative barycenter accuracy. Substantial iteration reductions and reported inference speedups of 1.25–7.4× suggest practical value for repeated OT computations.

Proposition 5 provides a useful residual bound motivating training without converged target potentials. The manuscript also supplies extensive implementation details, training costs, and links to code and pretrained weights, and explicitly acknowledges limitations in resolution extrapolation.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification mixes incompatible dual-potential conventions. For the dual in Equation (3), which uses the reference measure µ⊗ν, the coupling is Πij = µiνj exp((fi+gj−Cij)/ε). Proposition 1 instead identifies the Sinkhorn scalings directly with exp(f/ε) and exp(g/ε). Consequently, the learned ε log(v) differs from the potential covered by Proposition 2 by ε log(ν), up to a constant; the stated convergence theorem therefore does not directly justify convergence of the implemented targets. Equation (1) also has the wrong KL sign, and Algorithm 1 labels the transport-only cost as the regularized objective. These conventions need reconciliation to establish precisely what is predicted and evaluated.

The principal universality claim is not established for the implemented generator. Theorem 3 assumes equal input/output dimensions and Lip(NNθ) < λ, whereas Appendix C specifies a 200-dimensional latent input, 8192 output entries, and no enforcement of the Lipschitz constraint. Although the appendix acknowledges these differences, its conclusion that the theorem rules out generator coverage as a bottleneck does not follow. Moreover, full support for an idealized generator would establish expressivity, not uniform accuracy of the trained solver.

The downstream optimization procedures contain substantive correctness problems as written. Algorithm 3 applies softmax directly to updated probability masses: even with one target and µ already equal to that target, the gradient vanishes but softmax(µ) generally changes µ. Equation (11) omits the derivative of the outer self-interaction term −½OTε(µ̂,µ̂), so it does not describe the claimed Sinkhorn-divergence gradient flow. The implemented variables and objectives need clarification and corrected validation. The broad claim of superior geodesic prediction also rests on a single illustrated comparison with GeONet rather than aggregate measurements.

The experiments do not isolate the contributions of the proposed training choices. Controlled comparisons against a fixed synthetic sampler, alternative target objectives, and a baseline trained on the same generated distributions are missing. Comparing against Meta OT trained only on MNIST demonstrates transfer beyond that training distribution, but does not determine how much improvement comes from broader training data versus the proposed architecture and adversarial bootstrapping. The qualitative MLP discussion does not resolve this attribution.

The headline runtime comparison uses a 1% error threshold relative to an already known transport cost. This cannot serve as a stopping rule in deployment and does not ensure comparable transport-plan feasibility. Figures 18–19 provide helpful marginal-error evidence, but timings at matched marginal-residual or duality-gap tolerances are needed. Timing comparisons with Gaussian initialization and Meta OT on the same implementation and hardware, together with an amortization analysis of the approximately 35-hour training cost per model, would better substantiate the practical efficiency claim.

strengths: Combining neural operators, synthetic adversarial training, and short Sinkhorn bootstrapping is a useful approach to amortizing optimal transport across problems. Supporting variable resolutions extends the fixed-input setting of Meta OT while retaining standard Sinkhorn refinement.

The experiments demonstrate promising generalization without training on the evaluation datasets. Table 4 reports 1.3% error on CIFAR versus 23.1% for MNIST-trained Meta OT. Multiple datasets, cross-dataset pairs, three cost/domain settings, and resolution sweeps provide substantial empirical coverage within the image-grid setting.

Evaluation extends beyond transport-cost prediction. The marginal-constraint results and quantitative barycenter comparison provide useful evidence for downstream computations: Table 6 reports barycenter error of 0.021 for UNOT, versus 0.033 for Gaussian initialization and 0.057 for Ones.

The paper provides detailed hyperparameters, training budgets, pseudocode, and a code/model-weight link. Proposition 5 gives a useful residual-to-potential-error bound that motivates learning from short Sinkhorn refinements.
weaknesses: The central generator-universality claim is not established for the implemented method. Theorem 3 requires equal latent/output dimensions and a Lipschitz constraint, whereas Appendix C uses a 200-dimensional latent for up to 8192 output entries and explicitly does not enforce the constraint. This locally Lipschitz low-dimensional generator cannot have the full-dimensional density established by the theorem. The appendix acknowledges the mismatch but nevertheless concludes that generator coverage cannot limit performance; that conclusion does not follow.

The continuum theory and numerical targets use inconsistent dual-potential conventions. Equation (3), used by Proposition 2, gives coupling entries μ_i ν_j exp((f_i + g_j − C_ij)/ε), whereas Proposition 1 and Algorithm 1 use counting-measure Sinkhorn scalings. Consequently, the predicted ε log(v) differs from the corresponding relative-KL potential by ε log(ν), up to a gauge constant. This missing conversion matters under resolution changes, so Proposition 2 does not directly justify convergence of the learned targets. Separately, Equation (1) has the wrong KL sign, and Algorithm 1 labels the transport-only cost as the regularized objective.

The experiments do not isolate the benefits of adversarial generation and the bootstrapped loss. Missing controls include an otherwise identical FNO trained on fixed or random synthetic measures and a comparison against training with the dual objective. Meta OT receives MNIST-only training rather than similarly diverse synthetic training, so its out-of-distribution failure confounds training coverage with methodological differences. These controls would substantiate why the proposed combination produces the gains.

The strongest runtime claim uses a stopping criterion based on 1% error against the known transport cost, which is unavailable during deployment. The appendix's marginal-constraint curves are helpful, but wall-clock comparisons at matched marginal-residual or duality-gap tolerances are missing, as are timings against competing initializers. An amortization analysis would also clarify when the stated 35-hour training cost per model becomes worthwhile. The results support benchmark acceleration more convincingly than the broad state-of-the-art speed claim.

Some downstream computations are incorrect as written. Equation (11) omits the derivative of the outer Sinkhorn divergence's source self-interaction term. Algorithm 3 applies softmax directly to the current probability vector minus a gradient; this is neither a simplex projection nor an exponentiated-gradient update and generally does not leave an optimum fixed. These formulas need correction and reconciliation with the implementation before the geometry experiments can be reproduced reliably.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: amortizing repeated optimal transport computations. Combining Fourier Neural Operators, adversarially generated training measures, and bootstrapped Sinkhorn targets is a meaningful contribution that extends learned initialization beyond a fixed dataset and resolution.

The reported results provide substantial evidence of effective initialization on the tested distributions. Table 4 reports 1.3–2.8% mean transport-cost errors after one Sinkhorn iteration, with large improvements over MNIST-trained Meta OT outside MNIST. The iteration counts and marginal-violation curves provide additional evidence beyond scalar cost prediction.

The evaluation includes three cost/domain settings, resolution sweeps, an epsilon-conditioned variant, and downstream barycenter experiments. Table 6's quantitative barycenter comparison is particularly useful for assessing whether predicted potentials support applications beyond distance estimation.

Proposition 5 provides a useful contraction-based rationale for the bootstrapping objective. The architecture descriptions, hyperparameter tables, and links to code and model weights also support understanding and reproduction.
weaknesses: The central universality claim is not established for the implemented generator. Theorem 3 requires equal input/output dimensions and a residual network with Lipschitz constant below the skip coefficient. Appendix C instead describes a 200-dimensional latent input producing up to 8192 outputs, without enforcing the Lipschitz condition. Acknowledging these differences does not justify the subsequent claim that generator coverage cannot be a bottleneck. The theorem should be connected to an implementation satisfying its assumptions, or the universality claims substantially narrowed; positive density alone would also not establish adequate coverage during finite training.

The OT definitions and potential conventions need reconciliation. Equation (1) subtracts KL, whereas the convex Sinkhorn problem requires adding it. The KL-reference dual in Equation (3) requires marginal factors when converting potentials into the scaling vectors of Proposition 1. Algorithm 1 then reports only the transport term, although Appendix A.7 defines OTε using the regularized objective. These distinctions affect objective values, potential normalization, and derivatives. The paper needs explicit conversions showing that Proposition 2 applies to the potentials actually learned and clarifying exactly which quantity the experiments evaluate.

The downstream optimization formulas contain substantive problems as written. Algorithm 3 applies softmax directly to the probability vector after subtracting its gradient; even at zero gradient, this changes a nonuniform optimum, so it is not the stated projected gradient method. Equation (11) also omits the derivative of the outer Sinkhorn divergence's source self-interaction term. These issues require corrected algorithms and verification of the implemented computations before the claimed barycenter and Wasserstein-gradient-flow interpretations are convincing.

The experiments do not isolate the contributions of adversarial generation and the bootstrapping loss. Comparisons against a fixed synthetic generator, an FNO trained with the dual objective, and a baseline trained on comparable synthetic data would distinguish architectural benefits from differences in training distributions and objectives. The qualitative MLP discussion does not replace these controls. Likewise, the broad claim of superiority over GeONet rests on a single illustrated geodesic rather than aggregate quantitative evaluation.

The strongest efficiency claim remains incompletely supported. The 7.4× speedup is measured against the default initialization using an oracle 1% transport-cost-error threshold. Marginal-violation plots are helpful, but wall-clock comparisons against stronger initializers at shared, practically available stopping tolerances are missing. The 35-hour training cost also warrants an amortization discussion. The evidence supports useful acceleration in the reported setting more clearly than a general claim of leading solver performance.
